newsitem.title: USA: GM CEO Smith hopeful for labor pact in Michigan.
newsitem.headline: GM CEO Smith hopeful for labor pact in Michigan.

text.p: General Motors Corp. Chairman Jack Smith said Friday he hopes to reach a deal to avoid a strike by the United Auto Workers union at two Michigan transmission plants that could shut down much of GM's North American operations.
Smith said negotiations are continuing with UAW Local 735, which represents about 5,300 workers at two GM plants in Ypsilanti and Romulus, Mich.
The union has set a strike deadline for 11:59 p.m. EDT (0359 GMT) Friday.
"We're still hopeful we'll reach an agreement," Smith told reporters following a dedication ceremony of GM's new Service Parts Operations world headquarters here.

The two plants, part of GM's Powertrain Division, make a variety of front-wheel drive and rear-wheel drive transmissions and related components. A strike at the plants could quickly affect GM's North American assembly and parts operations.

Responding to questions about the future of GM's Buick City car assembly plant in Flint, Smith said the automaker will continue to have a major presence in Michigan's Genesee County, which includes the city of Flint and surrounding areas. But, he said the company's operations there need to remain competitive by global standards.
"We've got huge operations here. I don't see them disappearing," he said, adding, "They need to be competitive."

GM has not scheduled any new production at the Buick City plant beyond 1999, when production of the Buick LeSabre and Pontiac Bonneville sedans is slated to end, leading to speculation that the plant will be closed.
At the same time, GM has announced plans to expand its truck plant in Flint to build medium-duty trucks and commercial versions of its pick-up trucks.
Separately, Smith said GM has launched a capacity study for its global operations to determine how the company can remain competitive in both mature and developing markets around the world.
"It's looking at the balance. How we remain competitive in our mature markets and how we grow in the new and expanding markets," he said.
